supplied_texts.title: The Ferry (prose extract, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Anonymous
supplied_texts.text:
The ferry was late, as it was every Thursday, and Mrs Okafor stood at the rail with her hat in both hands so that the wind could not have it. Below her the water was the colour of a bruise that had begun to heal. Across the harbour, the town she had left forty years before assembled itself out of the mist: first the church, then the chimney of the old cannery, then, last and smallest, the row of white houses where her sister still lived and still did not write.

'You'll want to sit down, madam,' said the boy who took the tickets. 'It gets rough by the point.'

'I have been rough by the point before,' she said, and did not sit.

She had brought a cake in a tin. On the train she had rehearsed three different first sentences, and she had discarded each of them at a different station. Now, with the town growing larger, she found that she had none at all, only the weight of the tin and the cold coming up through her good shoes.

Also the writer uses a list, "first the church, then the chimney of the old cannery", to show the town appearing. When the boy tells her to sit down she says "I have been rough by the point before" which shows she is stubborn and strong. At the end she has "only the weight of the tin and the cold in her good shoes" which shows she is nervous because she has nothing to say. Overall the writer presents Mrs Okafor as nervous but strong.

Task — Paper 1, SL — How does the writer present Mrs Okafor's feelings about returning home?
What the task wants: a close analysis of how the writer's word choices and structure present Mrs Okafor's feelings about going back to the town she left.
What earned credit: the bruise image is read as hurt that is healing ("could mean that she has been hurt"), which goes beyond the literal scene; and the line "I have been rough by the point before" is quoted exactly.
Provisional marks: A 3/5 · B 2/5 · C 2–3/5 · D 3/5 — total 10–11/20 — provisional
Biggest gap: each quotation is followed by what it "shows", a feeling or a trait, but no key word is analysed, so the paragraph names Mrs Okafor's feelings instead of showing how the writer presents them.
Fix it: 1. Choose one key word in each quotation, say what it means and what it does here, and only then state the feeling it produces; replace "which shows" with that explanation. 2. Add the evidence that answers "returning home" directly: she "rehearsed three different first sentences" and "discarded each of them at a different station", and her sister "still did not write". Your paragraph mentions neither the sister nor the forty years. 3. Quote and name accurately: the bruise comparison has no "like" or "as", so it is a metaphor, and the last quotation should read "the cold coming up through her good shoes", not "the cold in her good shoes".

The bruise sentence is the one place that explains how an image works.
- C 2–3: the focus is set in the first sentence, but the evidence follows the text's order, linked by "Also" and "When", and the feeling shifts between nervous, sad and stubborn.
- D 3: generally clear and accurate; terminology is thin and one term is misapplied; "which shows" repeats.

supplied_texts.text:
The ferry was late, as it was every Thursday, and Mrs Okafor stood at the rail with her hat in both hands so that the wind could not have it. Below her the water was the colour of a bruise that had begun to heal. Across the harbour, the town she had left forty years before assembled itself out of the mist: first the church, then the chimney of the old cannery, then, last and smallest, the row of white houses where her sister still lived and still did not write.

'You'll want to sit down, madam,' said the boy who took the tickets. 'It gets rough by the point.'

'I have been rough by the point before,' she said, and did not sit.

She had brought a cake in a tin. On the train she had rehearsed three different first sentences, and she had discarded each of them at a different station. Now, with the town growing larger, she found that she had none at all, only the weight of the tin and the cold coming up through her good shoes.

$= 4788$ euros, to the nearest euro (A1)

**Part (b) — find — 3 marks**

recorded_answer.question: I'm a Computer Science SL student (the course first assessed in May 2027; my exams are in May 2027), Python option. Paper 2 practice using the supplied code and list. (a) Copy and complete a trace table for find_position(scores, 67), showing low, high, mid and steps on each pass of the loop. [4] (b) State the value returned by find_position(scores, 20). [2] (c) Explain why the list must be sorted for this algorithm to work. [2] (d) Compare the maximum number of passes this algorithm needs for a sorted list of 1,000 items with the maximum number of comparisons a linear search needs. [3]
recorded_answer.response_text:
(a) [4]

Here low and high are the values at the start of each pass.

| Pass | low | high | mid | items[mid] | steps | Test and update |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | 0 | 9 | — | — | 0 | low <= high (0 <= 9), so the loop runs |
| 1 | 0 | 9 | 4 | 38 | 1 | 38 = 67? no; 38 < 67, so low = 5 |
| 2 | 5 | 9 | 7 | 67 | 2 | 67 = 67, so return mid, steps |

The function returns (7, 2): the value 67 is at index 7 and is found on pass 2.

(b) [2]

(-1, 3)

The passes test mid = 4, 1 and 2. The loop ends when low (2) is greater than high (1), so 20 is not in the list and the function returns -1 with 3 steps.

(c) [2]

Binary search discards half of the list on each pass by comparing the target with the middle item. That comparison tells the algorithm which half to keep only when the list is sorted in ascending order. If items[mid] < target, every item to the left of mid is smaller too, so the target can only lie to the right, and low = mid + 1 is safe. In an unsorted list, a smaller middle item says nothing about the items on its left, so the half that holds the target may be discarded. For example, with [9, 3, 7] and target 9: mid = 1 gives 3 < 9, so low moves to 2; the next middle item is 7, so low moves to 3, the loop ends and the function returns -1, although 9 is at index 0.

(d) [3]

Binary search: at most 10 passes. Linear search: at most 1,000 comparisons. Both are worst-case counts for the same 1,000 items, each of the operation its algorithm repeats.

Binary search working: each pass removes the middle item and one half of the rest, so at most half of the remaining items are left. The worst-case number of items still to search is 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1 → 0. That is 10 passes, and no more are possible, because after 10 passes fewer than one item remains (1,000 ÷ 2^10 = 0.98). A target larger than every item reaches this worst case.

Linear search working: the worst case is a target that is the last item or is absent, so all 1,000 items are compared.

A pass makes up to two value comparisons (== and <), so the binary search makes at most 20 comparisons. That is still far fewer than 1,000.

A Business Management student will use your answer to analyse a drinks producer, so state each result clearly with its units. (i) Calculate the price elasticity of demand for sugar-sweetened drinks between 2024 and 2025. [2] (ii) Calculate the government's tax revenue in 2025. [1] (iii) Calculate the tax burden per litre and in total for consumers and for producers in 2025. [2] (iv) Calculate the change in producers' revenue, after tax, between 2024 and 2025. [2] (v) Using a diagram, explain why consumers bear most of the burden of this tax. [3] Write no more than 350 words, plus working and your diagram.
recorded_answer.response_text:
(i) [2 marks]

Measure: price elasticity of demand (PED) for sugar-sweetened drinks, 2024 to 2025, using the price paid by consumers.
Percentage change in quantity demanded = (105 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = −12.50%
Percentage change in price = (1.90 − 1.60) ÷ 1.60 × 100 = 18.75%
PED = −12.50 ÷ 18.75 = −0.67
Result: PED = −0.67. Demand is price inelastic, because its absolute value, 0.67, is less than 1.

(ii) [1 mark]

Tax revenue, 2025 = tax per litre × quantity sold after the tax = $0.40 × 105 million litres = $42 million per year.
Result: government tax revenue in 2025 was $42 million per year.

(iii) [2 marks]

Measure: tax burden per litre and in total, 2025, for consumers and for producers.
Pre-tax price, 2024 (no tax): P₁ = $1.60 per litre
Price paid by consumers, 2025: Pc = $1.90 per litre
Price received by producers, 2025: Pp = $1.90 − $0.40 = $1.50 per litre
Consumers: ($1.90 − $1.60) = $0.30 per litre; $0.30 × 105 million litres = $31.50 million per year
Producers: ($1.60 − $1.50) = $0.10 per litre; $0.10 × 105 million litres = $10.50 million per year
Check: $31.50 million + $10.50 million = $42.00 million per year, equal to the tax revenue in (ii).
Result: consumers bear $0.30 per litre, or $31.50 million per year (75% of the tax); producers bear $0.10 per litre, or $10.50 million per year (25% of the tax).

(iv) [2 marks]

Measure: producers' revenue after tax = price received by producers × quantity sold.
2024 = $1.60 × 120 million litres = $192.00 million per year (no tax, so the price received equals the price paid)
2025 = $1.50 × 105 million litres = $157.50 million per year
Change = $157.50 million − $192.00 million = −$34.50 million per year
Percentage change = −34.50 ÷ 192.00 × 100 = −17.97%
Check: consumer spending in 2025 = $1.90 × 105 million litres = $199.50 million = $157.50 million + $42.00 million tax revenue.
Result: producers' revenue after tax fell by $34.50 million per year (17.97%) between 2024 and 2025.

(v) [3 marks]

Diagram 1: The market for sugar-sweetened drinks in Varenland, with a $0.40 per litre tax
Axes: vertical — Price ($ per litre); horizontal — Quantity of sugar-sweetened drinks (million litres per year)
Curves: D, downward sloping; S₁, upward sloping; S₂, parallel to S₁ and $0.40 per litre above it
Change: the tax shifts supply up from S₁ to S₂ by $0.40 per litre (arrow from S₁ to S₂)
Equilibria: before the tax, P₁ = $1.60 at Q₁ = 120 million litres; after it, Pc = $1.90 paid by consumers and Pp = $1.50 received by producers, at Q₂ = 105 million litres
Areas: the rectangle between P₁ and Pc over Q₂ is the consumers' burden ($0.30 × 105 million litres); the rectangle between Pp and P₁ over Q₂ is the producers' burden ($0.10 × 105 million litres)

Consumers bear most of the tax because demand is relatively price inelastic: a PED of −0.67 means that the quantity bought falls by proportionally less than the price rises (12.50% against 18.75%). In Diagram 1 the tax shifts supply up from S₁ to S₂, and the market settles at 105 million litres, where consumers pay Pc = $1.90 and producers keep Pp = $1.50. Consumers therefore pay $0.30 of the $0.40 tax per litre, and producers absorb only $0.10. The data give demand's elasticity but not supply's, so the claim that demand responds less than supply is inferred from this split rather than measured.

(i) Calculate the price elasticity of demand for sugar-sweetened drinks between 2024 and 2025. [2] (ii) Calculate the government's tax revenue in 2025. [1] (iii) Calculate the tax burden per litre and in total for consumers and for producers in 2025. [2] (iv) Calculate the change in producers' revenue, after tax, between 2024 and 2025. [2] (v) Using a diagram, explain why consumers bear most of the burden of this tax. [3] Write no more than 350 words, plus working and your diagram.
recorded_answer.response_text:
(i) [2 marks]

Measure: price elasticity of demand (PED) for sugar-sweetened drinks, 2024 to 2025, using the price paid by consumers.
Percentage change in quantity demanded = (105 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = −12.50%
Percentage change in price = (1.90 − 1.60) ÷ 1.60 × 100 = 18.75%
PED = −12.50 ÷ 18.75 = −0.67
Result: PED = −0.67. Demand is price inelastic, because its absolute value, 0.67, is less than 1.

(ii) [1 mark]

Tax revenue, 2025 = tax per litre × quantity sold after the tax = $0.40 × 105 million litres = $42 million per year.
Result: government tax revenue in 2025 was $42 million per year.

(iii) [2 marks]

Measure: tax burden per litre and in total, 2025, for consumers and for producers.
Pre-tax price, 2024 (no tax): P₁ = $1.60 per litre
Price paid by consumers, 2025: Pc = $1.90 per litre
Price received by producers, 2025: Pp = $1.90 − $0.40 = $1.50 per litre
Consumers: ($1.90 − $1.60) = $0.30 per litre; $0.30 × 105 million litres = $31.50 million per year
Producers: ($1.60 − $1.50) = $0.10 per litre; $0.10 × 105 million litres = $10.50 million per year
Check: $31.50 million + $10.50 million = $42.00 million per year, equal to the tax revenue in (ii).
Result: consumers bear $0.30 per litre, or $31.50 million per year (75% of the tax); producers bear $0.10 per litre, or $10.50 million per year (25% of the tax).

(iv) [2 marks]

Measure: producers' revenue after tax = price received by producers × quantity sold.
2024 = $1.60 × 120 million litres = $192.00 million per year (no tax, so the price received equals the price paid)
2025 = $1.50 × 105 million litres = $157.50 million per year
Change = $157.50 million − $192.00 million = −$34.50 million per year
Percentage change = −34.50 ÷ 192.00 × 100 = −17.97%
Check: consumer spending in 2025 = $1.90 × 105 million litres = $199.50 million = $157.50 million + $42.00 million tax revenue.
Result: producers' revenue after tax fell by $34.50 million per year (17.97%) between 2024 and 2025.

(v) [3 marks]

Diagram 1: The market for sugar-sweetened drinks in Varenland, with a $0.40 per litre tax
Axes: vertical — Price ($ per litre); horizontal — Quantity of sugar-sweetened drinks (million litres per year)
Curves: D, downward sloping; S₁, upward sloping; S₂, parallel to S₁ and $0.40 per litre above it
Change: the tax shifts supply up from S₁ to S₂ by $0.40 per litre (arrow from S₁ to S₂)
Equilibria: before the tax, P₁ = $1.60 at Q₁ = 120 million litres; after it, Pc = $1.90 paid by consumers and Pp = $1.50 received by producers, at Q₂ = 105 million litres
Areas: the rectangle between P₁ and Pc over Q₂ is the consumers' burden ($0.30 × 105 million litres); the rectangle between Pp and P₁ over Q₂ is the producers' burden ($0.10 × 105 million litres)

Consumers bear most of the tax because demand is relatively price inelastic: a PED of −0.67 means that the quantity bought falls by proportionally less than the price rises (12.50% against 18.75%). In Diagram 1 the tax shifts supply up from S₁ to S₂, and the market settles at 105 million litres, where consumers pay Pc = $1.90 and producers keep Pp = $1.50. Consumers therefore pay $0.30 of the $0.40 tax per litre, and producers absorb only $0.10. The data give demand's elasticity but not supply's, so the claim that demand responds less than supply is inferred from this split rather than measured.

Assume that all other factors affecting the demand for and the supply of sugar-sweetened drinks were unchanged between 2024 and 2025.
